title: Missing timestamp components for EXTRACT
body:
The EXTRACT method on timestamps (and date, time, timestamp_tz) are missing fields:

TIME:
- subsecond

DATE:
- iso_year
- us_year
- day_of_year
- monday_day_of_week
- sunday_day_of_week
- monday_week
- sunday_week
- iso_week
- us_week
- unix_time

TIMESTAMP_TZ:
- timezone_offset

all the fields missing from time or date are also missing from:
TIMESTAMP_SEC
TIMESTAMP_MS
TIMESTAMP_US
TIMESTAMP_NS

Descriptions that provide some more context for these fields/components:
```yml
* SUBSECOND Return number of microseconds since the last full second of the given timestamp.

* ISO_YEAR Return the ISO 8601 week-numbering year. First week of an ISO year has the majority (4 or more) of its
  days in January.
* US_YEAR Return US epidemiological year. First week of US epidemiological year has the majority (4 or more) of
  its days in January. Last week of US epidemiological year has the year's last Wednesday in it.
  US epidemiological week starts on Sunday.
* DAY_OF_YEAR Return the day of year (1 to 366). January 1st maps to day number 1, February 1st to 32, etc.
* MONDAY_DAY_OF_WEEK Return the day of week from Monday (1) to Sunday (7).
* SUNDAY_DAY_OF_WEEK Return the day of week from Sunday (1) to Saturday (7).
* MONDAY_WEEK Return week of year number (1-53). First week starts on first Monday of January.
* SUNDAY_WEEK Return week of year number (1-53). First week starts on first Sunday of January.
* ISO_WEEK Return ISO week of year number (1-53). First ISO calendar week has the majority (4 or more) of its
  days in January. ISO week starts on Monday.
* US_WEEK Return ISO-like week of year number (1-53). First US calendar week has the majority (4 or more) of its days in January. US week starts on Sunday.
* UNIX_TIME Return number of seconds that have elapsed since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, ignoring leap seconds.

* TIMEZONE_OFFSET Return number of seconds of timezone offset to UTC.
```

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
Hmm a lot of this functionality is [already there](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/functions/datepart) just with slightly different names (we use the [Postgres part names](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/functions-datetime.html#FUNCTIONS-DATETIME-EXTRACT)). But adding some aliases is not difficult. Others are trivial arithmetic (e.g., `MONDAY_DAY_OF_WEEK` is `SUNDAY_DAY_OF_WEEK` plus some modular arithmetic) and should probably be addressed as built in macros.

Where did this list come from?

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
@participant2 now that I have you here, I actually have a question about substrait that you might be able to answer
`sunday_day_of_week` says it returns 1-indexed days, ours is 0-indexed (result for sunday is 0)

Which means we have to transform this to `dayofweek(x)+1` to comply to the substrait spec.
Because of this, the result will be different between the substrait compiled query, and our original query.
If I was a user of this I would expect that to not be the case, that I only have to compile it to substrait to run my query on another dbms.

But now I need to compile it to substrait even before I want to run it on another dbms, if I want the guarantee that the results will be the same.
Is that expected behavior?

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
1-indexed encoding was chosen because that's [ISO8601 encoding](https://<redacted-host>/w/cpp/chrono/weekday/encoding).  If you can argue that most systems are 0-indexed, then spec could still be changed (it's early enough it wouldn't be too disrupting). Or you could propose to add 0-indexed variants which would not be a breaking change.

As per my understanding Substrait doesn't aim to model SQL exactly, but rather to provide enough primitives to express all of it's dialects. That unfortunately means glue layers (`dayofweek(x)+1`). I also don't think substrait is intended for end users, just dbms devs, so your users would ideally not be exposed to tho this discrepancy :). So if I understood correctly it is expected behavior.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
> 1-indexed encoding was chosen because that's [ISO8601 encoding](https://<redacted-host>/w/cpp/chrono/weekday/encoding). If you can argue that most systems are 0-indexed, then spec could still be changed (it's early enough it wouldn't be too disrupting). Or you could propose to add 0-indexed variants which would not be a breaking change.

[MS-SQL](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/functions/datepart-transact-sql?view=sql-server-ver16#week-and-weekday-datepart-arguments), [DB2](https://<redacted-host>/docs/en/db2-for-zos/12?topic=functions-dayofweek), [Snowflake](https://<redacted-host>/en/sql-reference/functions-date-time#label-supported-date-time-parts), and [Clickhouse](https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/sql-reference/functions/date-time-functions#todayofweek) all return 1-based weekdays (although some of them have an option to use 0).

Postgres is 0-based for non-ISO weekdays, but 1-based for ISO (we follow them). [SQLite](https://<redacted-host>/lang_datefunc.html) is 0-based, but it has to use `strftime(%w)`.

[Oracle](https://<redacted-host>/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/19/sqlrf/EXTRACT-datetime.html#GUID-36E52BF8-945D-437D-9A3C-6860CABD210E) doesn't support weekday extraction.

There is also the issue of what the start of the week is set to (we use ICU, and it is configurable, but we only use it for ISO week arithmetic). It is worth mentioning that [ICU is 1-based](https://unicode-org.github.io/icu-docs/apidoc/dev/icu4c/ucal_8h.html#a62d9fe551bd48e4141fce52b917119a4)

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
Sorry, I can't find if ISO defines indexing for weeks starting on Sunday. We could change to:
```
* MONDAY_DAY_OF_WEEK Return the day of week from Monday (1) to Sunday (7).
* SUNDAY_DAY_OF_WEEK Return the day of week from Sunday (0) to Saturday (6).
```
Which then always makes Monday-Saturday 1-6 and Sunday index would change depending on the mode.

comments.author: participant1
participant2
comments.body:
> 			return isodow % 7;

Isn't modulo more expensive that a `x+1`? :)

Maximal set of functions would be:
```
* MONDAY_1_DAY_OF_WEEK Return the day of week from Monday (1) to Sunday (7).
* MONDAY_0_DAY_OF_WEEK Return the day of week from Monday (0) to Sunday (6).
* SUNDAY_0_DAY_OF_WEEK Return the day of week from Sunday (0) to Saturday (6).
* SUNDAY_1_DAY_OF_WEEK Return the day of week from Sunday (1) to Saturday (7).
```
Options are:
1. Propose a change to the maximal set
2. Propose a change to a subset (e.g. https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/issues/6805#issuecomment-1479746294)
3. Keep things as they are

I don't feel strongly about any of the options, we'd want a good argument for the change.

> Maximal set of functions would be:

> * MONDAY_0_DAY_OF_WEEK Return the day of week from Monday (0) to Sunday (6).

On the Substrait side, I think we could do this in a cleaner and more general way by simply adding a new option to the `extract` function to specify whether returned integer values should be 0-indexed or 1-indexed. This could pertain not just to days but also weeks, months, and quarters. Let's discuss this in https://github.com/substrait-io/substrait/issues/477.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: This stuff is usually handled in databases by sessions settings, which add another wrinkle to the substrait design: The same query can produce different results based on the user's session settings. One common example is the default ordering of `NULL`s, which a number of RDBMSes - inducing DuckDB - implement. Weekday settings are another.

comments.body: I think Substrait is stateless so these parameters will need to be passed at runtime.

comments.author: participant4
comments.body:
To me making this change at the Subtrait consumer/producer level makes the most sense. The DuckDB substrait consumer/producer knows DuckDB’s and Substrait’s semantics, and can add a +1 or -1 as required as part of the translation. Or is there a requirement that a function maps 1:1 at that level?

> Which means we have to transform this to dayofweek(x)+1 to comply to the substrait spec.
> Because of this, the result will be different between the substrait compiled query, and our original query.

I don’t quite follow why the result would be different- the producer would add a +1, and the consumer would add a -1. The end result of the query will then be the same as long as the consumer/producer both make the correct translation, no?

comments.author: participant2
comments.body: I've opened https://github.com/substrait-io/substrait/pull/479 to control indexing.

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
> To me making this change at the Subtrait consumer/producer level makes the most sense. The DuckDB substrait consumer/producer knows DuckDB’s and Substrait’s semantics, and can add a +1 or -1 as required as part of the translation. Or is there a requirement that a function maps 1:1 at that level?

There is no imperative for functions in Substrait to map 1:1 to functions in a Substrait-consuming engine like DuckDB.

> > Which means we have to transform this to dayofweek(x)+1 to comply to the substrait spec.
> > Because of this, the result will be different between the substrait compiled query, and our original query.
> 
> I don’t quite follow why the result would be different- the producer would add a +1, and the consumer would add a -1. The end result of the query will then be the same as long as the consumer/producer both make the correct translation, no?

Agreed. One of the main objectives of Substrait is to enable Substrait-producing APIs/DSLs to have the freedom to choose which conventions they want to follow (e.g. they can choose zero-based or one-based indexing) and to enable Substrait-consuming engines to execute plans and return results that are consistent with these conventions, or to throw an error if they cannot. It is expected that engines like DuckDB will have different behaviors when executing a plan from Substrait than when executing a plan from a query in their native query language or API. The behaviors need not match, but they should be made explicit.

comments.author: participant5
comments.body:
> This stuff is usually handled in databases by sessions settings, which add another wrinkle to the substrait design: The same query can produce different results based on the user's session settings. One common example is the default ordering of NULLs, which a number of RDBMSes - inducing DuckDB - implement. Weekday settings are another.

No existing function yet has been described to depend on session settings.  However, there was some discussion about it at some point (I think in the proposal for `random` which didn't make it through) so I won't rule it out entirely.

However, in this case, session settings should not be a wrinkle.  Once we clarify in Substrait whether these indices are 0-based or 1-based then there should be one answer that does not depend on session settings.

> To me making this change at the Subtrait consumer/producer level makes the most sense. The DuckDB substrait consumer/producer knows DuckDB’s and Substrait’s semantics, and can add a +1 or -1 as required as part of the translation. Or is there a requirement that a function maps 1:1 at that level?

If DuckDb is the only consumer that uses 1-based indexing, given that DuckDb can already consume and produce Substrait, I think it would be fine to handle it within DuckDb.  However, if there are other producers / consumers, then I think there is value in expressing the option.  There's pros & cons to both approaches.

* If you keep Substrait's option set limited then it is harder for consumers to adopt Substrait because they have to map everything to a single alternative dialect.
* If you make Substrait's option set very flexible then it is harder for producers to create plans that successfully run against consumers because the likelihood of incompatible options is high.

However, I think the goal of Substrait (and this is certainly open for discussion) is to lean towards a flexible option set with the hopes that translators eventually emerge which centralize all of these +1/-1 translations in a single point.
